\begin{proof}
Assume for contradiction that $G$ is simple. For each prime $p\mid |G|$, Sylow's theorem gives
\[
n_p\equiv1\pmod p,
\qquad n_p\mid |G|/p.
\]
For $p=13$, $n_{13}\mid105$ and $n_{13}\equiv1\pmod{13}$, so $n_{13}=1$ or $105$. Simplicity excludes $n_{13}=1$, hence $n_{13}=105$.

For $p=7$, $n_7\mid195$ and $n_7\equiv1\pmod7$, so $n_7=1$ or $15$; thus $n_7=15$. For $p=5$, $n_5\mid273$ and $n_5\equiv1\pmod5$, so $n_5=1$ or $21$; thus $n_5=21$.

Each Sylow subgroup of order $p$ has $p-1$ nonidentity elements, and distinct subgroups of order $p$ have no nonidentity elements in common. Moreover, elements counted for different primes have distinct orders. Therefore the numbers of elements of orders $13$, $7$, and $5$ are respectively
\[
105(12)=1260,\qquad15(6)=90,\qquad21(4)=84.
\]
This gives at least $1260+90+84=1434$ distinct elements, contradicting $|G|=1365$. Hence $G$ is not simple.
\end{proof}
